items.followUp: How does increasing temperature generally affect the solubility of solids and gases in water?

rubric.why: Most solid solutes become more soluble as temperature rises.
rubric.description: States the effect of increasing temperature on the solubility of most solids.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that solubility generally increases as temperature increases.

rubric.why: Gas solubility generally falls as temperature rises.
rubric.description: States the effect of increasing temperature on the solubility of gases.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that gas solubility generally decreases as temperature increases.

modelAnswer: The solubility of most solid solutes in a liquid increases with an increase in temperature.
The solubility of gases in liquids generally decreases with an increase in temperature.

items.followUp: Write any two physical properties of metals.

rubric.why: Poor electrical and thermal conductivity is a common physical property of non-metals.
rubric.description: Gives one valid physical property of non-metals, such as being poor conductors.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one correct property.

rubric.why: Non-metals have several other characteristic physical properties.
rubric.description: Gives a second valid physical property of non-metals.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct property distinct from the first.

modelAnswer: Non-metals are generally poor conductors of heat and electricity.
Solid non-metals are generally brittle and cannot be beaten into sheets.

items.followUp: What is meant by electropositive character?

rubric.why: Metallic character describes an atom's tendency to lose electrons.
rubric.description: States that metallic character is the tendency of an atom to lose electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the electron-loss idea.

rubric.why: Loss of electrons forms a positive ion, the defining result of metallic behaviour.
rubric.description: Connects electron loss with formation of a positive ion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the atom forms a positive ion or cation.

modelAnswer: Metallic character is the tendency of an atom to lose one or more electrons.
By losing electrons, the atom forms a positively charged ion (cation).

items.followUp: Define Chemistry and describe any four branches of Chemistry.

rubric.why: These are central parts of the textbook definition of Chemistry.
rubric.description: Defines Chemistry in terms of the study of matter and its composition, structure or properties.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a substantially correct definition.

rubric.why: Physical chemistry applies physical principles to chemical systems.
rubric.description: Describes physical chemistry.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one correct branch description.

rubric.why: Organic chemistry deals with carbon compounds.
rubric.description: Describes organic chemistry.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one correct branch description.

rubric.why: The response must describe two further branches accurately to complete the four requested branches.
rubric.description: Describes two additional branches of Chemistry.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for each of two correctly described additional branches.

modelAnswer: Chemistry is the branch of science that studies the composition, structure and properties of matter and the changes it undergoes.
Physical chemistry applies the principles of physics to chemical systems and reactions.
Organic chemistry is the study of carbon compounds.
Inorganic chemistry is the study of elements and their compounds, other than most carbon compounds.
Biochemistry is the study of the chemical substances and processes occurring in living organisms.

items.followUp: State four observations made in Rutherford's alpha-particle scattering experiment.

rubric.why: Most alpha particles passed through the foil without deflection.
rubric.description: States that most alpha particles passed straight through the foil.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this observation.

rubric.why: A small number of alpha particles were deflected through small angles.
rubric.description: States that some alpha particles were slightly deflected.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this observation.

rubric.why: A very small number were sharply deflected or turned back.
rubric.description: States that very few alpha particles were deflected through large angles or rebounded.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this observation.

rubric.why: The scattering results showed that the atom is mostly empty space and that its positive charge is concentrated in a small nucleus.
rubric.description: Gives a valid conclusion drawn from the experiment.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying mostly empty space or the small, positively charged nucleus.

modelAnswer: Most alpha particles passed through the gold foil without any deflection.
Some alpha particles were deflected through small angles.
Very few alpha particles were deflected through large angles or turned back.
These results showed that most of the atom is empty space and that its positive charge is concentrated in a small, dense nucleus.

items.followUp: Define a coordinate covalent bond and show its formation in H₃O⁺ and in NH₃→AlCl₃.

rubric.why: A coordinate covalent bond is a shared electron pair supplied by one atom.
rubric.description: Defines a coordinate covalent bond and identifies the donating atom's electron pair.
rubric.how: Award up to 2 marks: 1 for a shared pair and 1 for its donation by one atom to an acceptor.

rubric.why: In ammonium formation, nitrogen in ammonia donates its lone pair to H⁺.
rubric.description: Shows or explains formation of NH₄⁺ from NH₃ and H⁺.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the reactants/product and 1 mark for identifying nitrogen's lone-pair donation to H⁺.

rubric.why: Nitrogen in NH₃ donates a lone pair to electron-deficient boron in BF₃.
rubric.description: Shows or explains formation of the coordinate bond in NH₃→BF₃.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct donor–acceptor pairing or representation.

modelAnswer: A coordinate covalent bond is a covalent bond in which the shared pair of electrons is donated by one atom, the donor, to another atom, the acceptor.
In NH₃, nitrogen has a lone pair; it donates this pair to H⁺ to form ammonium: NH₃ + H⁺ → [H₃N→H]⁺ (NH₄⁺).
In BF₃, boron is electron-deficient; nitrogen in NH₃ donates its lone pair to boron: H₃N→BF₃.

items.followUp: Define vapour pressure and state three factors that affect it.

rubric.why: Vapour pressure is the pressure of vapour in equilibrium with its liquid at a given temperature.
rubric.description: Defines vapour pressure using equilibrium between liquid and vapour.
rubric.how: Award up to 2 marks for the vapour pressure/pressure idea and the equilibrium with the liquid.

rubric.why: Vapour pressure rises as temperature increases.
rubric.description: Identifies temperature as a factor affecting vapour pressure.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming temperature as a factor.

rubric.why: The liquid's nature and the strength of its intermolecular forces affect its tendency to evaporate.
rubric.description: Identifies the nature of the liquid and intermolecular forces as factors.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for each of these two factors.

modelAnswer: Vapour pressure is the pressure exerted by a vapour in equilibrium with its liquid in a closed container at a given temperature.
It depends on temperature: vapour pressure increases as temperature increases.
It depends on the nature or volatility of the liquid; more volatile liquids have higher vapour pressures.
It depends on intermolecular forces: stronger forces between particles give a lower vapour pressure.

items.followUp: Define an unsaturated solution and describe how a supersaturated solution can be prepared.

rubric.why: A saturated solution contains the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve at a specified temperature.
rubric.description: Defines a saturated solution with reference to the temperature and maximum dissolved solute.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the maximum-solute-at-a-given-temperature idea.

rubric.why: A supersaturated solution contains more dissolved solute than a saturated solution at the same temperature.
rubric.description: Defines a supersaturated solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the excess dissolved-solute idea at a specified temperature.

rubric.why: Heating allows additional solute to dissolve in the solution.
rubric.description: States that the solution is heated to dissolve extra solute.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the heating and extra-solute step.

rubric.why: Cooling the hot solution carefully can leave more solute dissolved than is normally soluble at the lower temperature.
rubric.description: States that the hot solution is cooled carefully to obtain the supersaturated solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the cooling step.

modelAnswer: A saturated solution contains the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve in a given amount of solvent at a particular temperature.
A supersaturated solution contains more dissolved solute than a saturated solution can normally hold at that temperature.
To prepare one, heat a saturated solution and dissolve some additional solute in it.
Then cool the hot solution slowly and undisturbed; the excess solute remains dissolved, forming a supersaturated solution.
